title: Four cases, one that holds
intro:
*Five minutes. Commit before you look.*

Four HRBPs took a case to Finance in the same quarter. Each wanted roughly the same amount of money. **One of these survives contact with a CFO.**

Don't ask which request is most deserving. Ask which numbers can carry the claim being made on them.

artifacts.label: Case A · the retention intervention
artifacts.body:
"Engineering attrition is at crisis levels — we've lost 50% of the platform team this year. A £40k retention package would pay for itself immediately given replacement costs of £2.1M."

*(The platform team has six people. Three left: one retired, one relocated with a partner, one was managed out.)*

artifacts.label: Case B · the extra layer
artifacts.body: "Removing the regional director layer saves £780k fully loaded, plus an estimated £120k–£300k in decision-latency and meeting time across the 40 people beneath it — I've used the low end. Biggest weakness: the latency figure comes from my own observation over four months, not measurement, and if it's overstated the case still holds on the £780k alone."

artifacts.label: Case C · the vacancy
artifacts.body: "The unfilled enterprise AE role is costing us £3.4M in lost revenue this year, based on quota attainment for the territory. Filling it is the single highest-ROI action available to this business."

artifacts.label: Case D · the program
artifacts.body: "Our manager capability program will improve engagement by 12 points and reduce regretted attrition by 18%, delivering £1.6M in value against a £200k investment — benchmarks from three published industry studies of similar programs."

reasoning:
**B holds, and it holds because of what it gives away.** It states the fully loaded figure with a conservative range on the soft component, chooses the low end, names its own weakest input before anyone asks — observation rather than measurement — and then does the thing that actually wins the argument: **shows the conclusion surviving without it.** That is the sensitivity test, volunteered. Finance can now argue about £120k instead of about whether to believe you.

**A is small numbers dressed as a crisis.** "50% attrition" and "three of six" are arithmetically identical and rhetorically opposite — and once you see the denominator, the composition destroys the claim: a retirement, a relocation, and a managed exit are three different phenomena, and at most one of them is regretted. The £2.1M replacement figure is six-person variance multiplied by a benchmark. This is the module's central failure mode, and note that AI would have produced the same number faster and with more decimal places.

**C attributes an entire territory's revenue to one vacancy.** The number may not even be wrong, but it claims the role is the sole cause of the shortfall — no share stated, no acknowledgment that territories underperform for many reasons. It invites exactly one question, and the case has no answer to it. A share, stated and arguable, would have survived.

**D is benchmark laundering.** Every figure comes from someone else's population: 12 points, 18%, £1.6M — none of it from this organization, and the causal chain (program → engagement → attrition → money) multiplies three uncertain steps into one confident total. "Three published industry studies" is the tell Module 3 taught you to read: whose sample, and what would falsify it?

The pattern: **the case that won was the one that argued against itself first.**
